newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Worldwide nuclear safety pact enters into force.
newsitem.headline: Worldwide nuclear safety pact enters into force.

text.p: The first international convention focusing on the safety of atomic reactors entered into force on Thursday, the United Nations nuclear watchdog agency said.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said 27 states had consented to be bound by the convention, including four of the five nuclear weapons powers -- Britain, China, France and Russia.
The United States, the other nuclear weapons power, was one of the first states to sign the convention but has not yet ratified it.
"The United States has no problem with the convention, it is just going through the legal process at the moment," a U.S. embassy official said.
The document, also ratified by Japan, South Korea, Hungary, Finland, and Romania, commits signatory states to ensure the safety of land-based civil nuclear power plants.
Lithuania, the country which produces most of its power through nuclear energy, has also ratified the convention.
A total of 476 nuclear power plants were operating or being built around the world in 1995.

The pact binds states to report on the status of current nuclear plants and any plans to expand the industry. Radiation protection, emergency procedures and the siting and design of new plants must also be outlined.

"Though the safe use of nuclear energy remains clearly a national responsibility, the convention signals the growing recognition of the global interdependence of safe nuclear development," IAEA chief Hans Blix said in a statement.
Work on the convention began in 1991 after communism crumbled in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, revealing potential safety risks posed by the region's ageing reactors.
Access to more scrutiny by Western nations was also a factor following the explosion and fire at Chernobyl in Ukraine in 1986 which spewed clouds of radiation across Europe.
Ukraine has signed the convention but the agreement has yet to be ratified by its parliament.
Signatories will be required to submit an immediate report on atomic installations and, if necessary, urgently carry out improvements to upgrade the safety of sites.
"If such upgrading cannot be achieved, plans should be implemented to shut down the nuclear installation as soon as practically possible," the convention says.
The document sets out a framework for a review of a nation's atomic sites by other countries.
Neighbouring states, in particular, may call for an urgent study if they are concerned about a reactor's safety and a possible radioactive fallout accident affecting their own people and crops.
